title: Speaking with the Tradition: Grad Students Study the Classical Languages
author: Nolan Ryan
summary: Nolan Ryan, a graduate student at Hillsdale, reports on why the Diana Davis Spencer Graduate School of Classical Education requires a classical language of its students. Program chair Benjamin Beier says classical schools prefer teachers familiar with Latin and Greek, that anything encountered in translation loses something, and that a liberal arts education has always been attentive to language, echoing the Renaissance return to wise texts in their original tongue. Most students take a six-week summer Latin intensive, and by the end even beginners are translating Augustine, Erasmus, Caesar and Cicero, though retention requires continued use. Graduate Aidan Jones notes that fluency in Latin and Greek was once expected of students entering college and calls a few conjugations a low bar. The piece closes on the tension between the theoretical and the practical: going ad fontes to Virgil and Augustine while preparing teachers who may end up leading schools.
points: Classical schools prefer teachers and leaders who know Latin and Greek, so Hillsdale makes a classical language a graduate requirement.
Beier argues that translation always loses something and that more than one language gives more pathways into understanding reality.
A six-week Latin intensive takes beginners to translating major authors, but gains fade without continued practice.
What looks demanding now, Latin fluency on arrival, was once an ordinary expectation of college students.
The programme holds the practical and the theoretical together: reading the ancients in their own language while forming teachers and school leaders.
quotes: Chairman and Associate Professor of Education Benjamin Beier acknowledges it is helpful for grad students to read texts in translation. Although, “there also needs to be some attention to a foreign language,” he adds, “because anytime you encounter something in translation, you’re losing something.

In the contemporary classical education movement, schools have placed an emphasis on the Trivium, the arts of language. To be proficient in these arts means that students need to be pushed beyond their mother tongue, Beier says.
Meanwhile, Ian Altenburg, M.A., ’26, was brand new to the language. They both elected to take the summer intensive in Latin to fulfill the program requirements.

Several grad students have continued honing their Latin skills, either by auditing undergrad courses or regularly finding time to read and speak Latin with Beier and others. “As with any language,” Jones says, “use it or lose it.

However, historically, this is “a pretty low bar to learn some conjugations and some Latin verbs,” he says. And, while he would not recommend studying Latin only for practical reasons, there are plenty of practical justifications for learning the language.

On the other hand, classical teachers might find themselves in school leadership positions. In those cases, having even a small acquaintance with classical languages, especially if they are part of a school’s curriculum, can be incredibly valuable for a healthy faculty culture.
